Unverified Evidence: Uses only the current repository and design article; it adds no claim of completed training, performance, or deployment.
Project at a Glance Deep Learning Modeling Textbook is a personal learning and practical validation project for organizing data preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and reproducibility as one traceable workflow. Instead of stopping at isolated tutorial code, the project defines a modeling standard that can be reused when new data arrives: frame the problem, run a controlled experiment, and explain the result.
The public repository currently exposes only limited implementation detail. This case study is therefore a design document based on the repository’s stated scope of preprocessing, training, evaluation, and reproducibility management. It does not claim a particular dataset size, model accuracy, completed training run, or production deployment. The directory structure and validation items below are target design criteria, not a list of finished features.
1. Background: Executable Code Is Not Yet a Trustworthy Experiment A deep-learning example can load data, train a model, and print an accuracy score in a single notebook. In engineering work, however, that output is useful only if the team can answer questions such as:
Which version of the data was used for training? Were training, validation, and test samples kept independent? Was the same preprocessing contract used during training and inference? Which baseline and metric justify the claim that the model improved? Can another run with the same settings reproduce a comparable conclusion? In a manufacturing application, which is more costly: a missed defect or a false alarm? The project treats these questions as part of the experiment itself, not documentation added after training. The primary goal is not to build the most complex network. It is to develop an experimental discipline that preserves the causal chain between data, configuration, code, and results.
Project Goals Separate preprocessing, training, and evaluation into explicit stages. Prevent data leakage and evaluation contamination before model selection. Record configuration, code, environment, and outputs together so experiments can be repeated. Interpret error types and business costs in addition to aggregate accuracy. Create a transfer framework from educational examples to manufacturing quality and equipment data. 2. Architecture and Workflow Design Deep-learning modeling is not one action called “training.” Each stage needs a clear input, output, and responsibility so that a failure can be localized. For that reason, the project models the path from source data to evaluation report as a feedback pipeline.
graph LR A["Raw Data"] --> B["Schema and Quality Checks"] B --> C["Train / Validation / Test Split"] C --> D["Preprocessing and Feature Transformation"] D --> E["Baseline Model"] E --> F["Deep-Learning Training"] F --> G["Fixed-Test Evaluation"] G --> H["Error Analysis"] H --> I["Model, Configuration, and Evaluation Records"] I -->|"Improvement hypothesis"| B This design was chosen for three practical reasons:
Leakage prevention: the split is fixed first, and preprocessing parameters are fitted only on training data. Comparable experiments: different model architectures use the same split and evaluation functions. Root-cause traceability: a performance change can be connected to data, preprocessing, architecture, or threshold decisions. A notebook is useful for exploration, but its hidden state and cell execution order can make results fragile. Moving repeatable preparation, training, and evaluation logic into functions or scripts creates an explicit execution contract and makes a later transition to production easier.
3. Technologies and Why They Were Chosen Python Python provides one language for data handling, model experiments, and evaluation automation. The learning focus is not memorizing one framework’s API. It is understanding the contracts between tensor shapes, data loaders, training loops, loss functions, and evaluation functions so the same reasoning can transfer across frameworks.
Deep-Learning Modeling The model is treated as one component of the problem-solving system. A simple rule or small baseline, a defensible split, and explicit error costs are defined before adding depth or parameters. This order makes it possible to determine whether added model complexity creates real value.
Experiment Management from an MLOps Perspective MLOps here does not mean that a large-scale deployment platform has already been built. It means applying operational discipline during training by recording:
a data snapshot or data-version identifier; train, validation, and test split rules; preprocessing settings and model hyperparameters; random seeds and the execution environment; model weights, evaluation metrics, and error-analysis outputs; and the relationship between a code commit and an experiment result. GitHub GitHub is used to version code and documentation and to preserve why the design changed. The current public repository alone is not sufficient to verify full experimental reproducibility; code, configuration, dependencies, and execution instructions still need to be expanded.
4. Recommended Repository Structure and Design Rationale The following layout is a target architecture for developing the repository into a reproducible learning and validation system. It does not describe the current implementation as complete.
Deep_Learning_Text_book/ ├─ README.md # Problem definition, run order, result interpretation ├─ configs/ # Data, model, and training configuration ├─ notebooks/ # Exploration and concept validation ├─ src/ │ ├─ data/ # Loading, validation, and splitting │ ├─ preprocessing/ # Shared training/inference transformations │ ├─ models/ # Model construction interfaces │ ├─ train.py # Training entry point │ └─ evaluate.py # Fixed evaluation entry point ├─ tests/ # Schema and preprocessing unit tests ├─ reports/ # Metrics, confusion matrices, and error cases └─ artifacts/ # Models and execution metadata Why Separate notebooks/ from src/ Notebooks are appropriate for inspecting distributions and testing a hypothesis quickly. Reusable preprocessing and training logic should then move into deterministic code with a fixed execution order. This separation reduces dependence on hidden notebook state without sacrificing fast exploration.
Why Keep configs/ Separate When learning rate, batch size, input dimensions, and other settings are scattered throughout code, it becomes difficult to explain which change affected a result. Keeping configuration separate and saving it alongside outputs makes experiment-to-experiment differences inspectable. This case study intentionally does not prescribe “best” values; they must be selected from the data and validation evidence.
Why Separate reports/ from artifacts/ Reports contain evidence for human review, such as metrics and representative errors. Artifacts contain reusable machine outputs, such as model weights and execution metadata. The separation clarifies what should be reviewed, what can be reloaded, and what must be retained for traceability.
5. Data and Implementation Flow 5.1 Define the Prediction and Evaluation Unit First Before selecting a model, define what one prediction represents: one image, multiple views of one product, or a time window from a machine. This choice determines the correct split and evaluation method. For manufacturing work, the definition should also state the cost of a missed defect, a false rejection, and delayed inference.
5.2 Preserve Raw Data and Validate the Schema Raw data remains immutable and is treated as a read-only reference. File paths, labels, equipment IDs, production dates, lots, and other metadata are checked for format, missing values, and duplicates. A metadata defect can mix samples incorrectly even when the image or sensor values themselves are valid, so schema validation comes before modeling.
5.3 Split Before Fitting Preprocessing Computing normalization values from the complete dataset or placing augmented versions of one sample into different sets leaks information. Train, validation, and test boundaries are fixed first; only parameters estimated from the training set are applied to validation and test data.
Manufacturing samples from the same machine, lot, or acquisition session may be highly similar. A random row split can therefore put near-duplicates from the same product into both training and test sets. Depending on the problem, the design evaluates group splits by equipment, lot, or time.
5.4 Establish a Simple Baseline A rule-based method or small model is created before introducing a complex network. The baseline is not intended to be the final performer. It is a reference point for determining whether later complexity actually adds measurable value.
5.5 Train from Recorded Configuration The data version, split rule, model configuration, training configuration, random seed, and runtime environment are bundled as one experiment record. Training loss is not reviewed in isolation; validation trends and signs of overfitting are recorded as well. The test set remains fixed and is not repeatedly reused for model selection.
5.6 Review Metrics Together with Error Cases For classification, accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and the confusion matrix are selected according to operational cost. If passing a defective item is the dominant risk, recall for the defect class and false-negative examples take priority. If excessive false alarms stop production, precision and alarm frequency must be considered as well.
5.7 Preserve More Than a Model File Each meaningful result should retain at least the following evidence:
Record Why It Matters Data identifier and split rule Confirms whether the evaluation population changed Code commit and configuration Reconstructs the implementation and conditions Training and validation curves Reveals overfitting, underfitting, or instability Per-class metrics and confusion matrix Exposes error types hidden by averages Representative error samples Produces the next data or model hypothesis Execution environment Explains library and hardware differences 6. Technical Challenges and Resolution Strategy Data Leakage The most dangerous failure is often not model code but a broken evaluation boundary. Duplicate samples, shared lots, common acquisition sessions, or future information must not cross sets. The split rule itself belongs in the configuration and evaluation report so it can be audited.
Class Imbalance Manufacturing quality datasets may contain many normal samples and few rare defects. Overall accuracy can look high even when every item is predicted as normal. The design compares per-class metrics, sampling strategies, loss weighting, and threshold adjustment on a fixed validation set instead of assuming one technique is universally superior.
Reproducibility versus Bit-for-Bit Identity Fixing a random seed does not guarantee identical numbers across hardware and library implementations. Reproducibility is therefore defined as the ability to rerun the same code, data, and settings, reach a comparable conclusion, and explain any variation, rather than requiring every floating-point value to match.
Strong Offline Metrics versus Shop-Floor Performance Lighting, material, sensor, and equipment conditions can differ from the training environment. Offline tests should be supplemented by condition-based slice evaluation, monitoring for change over time, inference-latency checks, and explicit failure handling before a model is considered operationally safe.
Experiment Proliferation When many hyperparameters change at once, it is easy to select only the highest score and lose the causal explanation. The project favors changing one hypothesis at a time and recording unsuccessful experiments as well, preventing the same failed idea from being repeated without context.
7. Validation Framework The target validation framework separates data, model, reproducibility, and operations rather than compressing every concern into one score.
Validation Layer Primary Question Example Checks Data Are inputs valid and evaluation boundaries independent? Schema, missing values, duplicates, label distribution, group leakage Model Does the model improve meaningfully over the baseline? Fixed split, per-class metrics, confusion matrix, error cases Reproducibility Can the experiment be explained and rerun? Configuration, seed, environment, code and data versions Operations Can the model fail safely under field conditions? Inference time, out-of-distribution inputs, failure handling, data drift Validation evidence is read according to the decision being made. In quality inspection, a missed defect and a false rejection carry different costs. In equipment anomaly detection, early warning and the operator’s ability to respond can be as important as a classification score.
8. Resume Relevance: Connecting AI Practice to Manufacturing Engineering Manufacturing root-cause analysis connects process conditions, equipment, material lots, working time, and inspection results. This project applies the same discipline to model development:
Preserve source evidence by separating raw field data from derived data. Control change points by recording code, configuration, and data-split changes as experiment units. Define inspection criteria by connecting model metrics to the cost of accepting a defect or rejecting a good item. Maintain traceability from a model result back to its data version and execution conditions. Analyze causes, not averages by reviewing errors by equipment, lot, time, or operating condition. Standardize repeatable work by documenting the modeling workflow like an engineering work standard. This perspective keeps AI from becoming an isolated research exercise. A model is one element of a manufacturing process; it becomes a useful quality-improvement tool only when data-collection conditions, decision thresholds, traceability, and failure response are designed together. For a resume, the project demonstrates systems thinking and verification discipline rather than claiming an unverified production deployment or headline accuracy figure.
9. Current Limitations The public repository does not yet expose enough code, data documentation, configuration, or execution results to substantiate the full project scope. No validated performance figures for a specific dataset and model are available, so model rankings or quantitative improvements cannot be claimed. Reproducible commands, dependency versions, and automated tests cannot be verified from the public materials alone. This case study does not claim field validation or operational results on proprietary manufacturing data. The current portfolio value is therefore the reasoning used to design and validate experiments, not the performance of a completed production model. 10. Improvement Roadmap Add a small, publishable example dataset and a precise problem definition. Separate data checks, training, and evaluation into independently executable modules. Document environment files and run commands for a clean first-time reproduction. Compare a baseline and at least one deep-learning model on the same split and metrics. Generate an evaluation report containing a confusion matrix and representative error cases. Add unit tests for preprocessing and data-leakage prevention rules. Run minimum tests on code changes and record intended use and limitations in a model card. Validate equipment-, lot-, and time-based split scenarios with an open manufacturing dataset. The most important result in deep-learning modeling is not one peak score. It is the ability to explain why a particular dataset and architecture were selected and whether the same procedure can verify that decision again. This project is intended to evolve into a long-term experimental repository that develops that standard and transfers it to manufacturing data problems.

Public PDD · Delivery Record

Goal Separate public and field data, compare model stages on the same metrics, and design a recall-first threshold with a reinspection policy.
Success F1, recall, and precision are reported together with threshold rationale, false-positive handling, and explicit production limits.

Unverified Evidence: The report's data, model-evolution, second-test, threshold, and final-metric slides support this record.
Portfolio summary: Problem–Role–Action–Result–Evidence Item Verified scope Problem Micro-defect features overlapped with normal surfaces, data was imbalanced, and accuracy alone did not represent the cost of passing a defective weld. Role I was responsible for evaluation-metric design and validation, including F1, recall, false-positive behavior, and threshold interpretation. Action The team separated roughly 60,000 AI-Hub images from 198 field images, compared a DenseNet baseline, a two-model combination, and a ResNet+DeiT ensemble, then reviewed a second test set and tuned the decision threshold to prioritize missed-defect control. Result On the recorded evaluation set and selected threshold, the report lists F1 93.10%, Recall 100%, and Precision 87.07%. These values do not establish production-wide generalization. Evidence The public report’s dataset, model-evolution, second-test, threshold, and final-metric slides; no dedicated public repository. Resume bullets Separated approximately 60,000 public welding images and 198 field images by learning/field-validation purpose instead of presenting them as one undifferentiated training set. Compared DenseNet, a two-model combination, and a ResNet+DeiT ensemble, then used second-test error review to tune the operating threshold around missed-defect cost. Recorded F1 93.10%, Recall 100%, and Precision 87.07% on the stated evaluation set and defined manual reinspection as the control for remaining false positives. Interview STAR Situation: Missing a small weld defect carried a higher quality risk than sending a normal part to reinspection, while accuracy could remain high under class imbalance. Task: Establish a comparable evaluation framework and a decision threshold aligned with that asymmetric risk. Action: Separate data sources, compare model stages on the same metrics, inspect mixed normal/defect regions in a second test, and search thresholds that retained recall. Result: The selected evaluation produced Recall 100%, F1 93.10%, and Precision 87.07%. I also documented that this is inspection-assistance evidence, not proof of autonomous production deployment. 1. Why this project was structured this way Manufacturing vision is not finished when a model outputs a class. A deployable quality decision must answer four questions:
What exactly counts as a defect? Which data was used for learning and which data checks field transfer? What is the cost of a false negative versus a false positive? Can a quality engineer review the evidence behind a wrong decision? My battery-assembly experience with laser and ultrasonic welding made the decision boundary the center of this project. The model architecture matters, but the operational threshold and reinspection rule determine how a model affects quality risk.
2. Data and evaluation flow flowchart LR A["AI-Hub public images\n~60,000"] --> B["label / quality checks"] B --> C["model comparison"] D["field images\n198"] --> E["field-condition check"] C --> E E --> F["probability outputs"] F --> G["threshold search"] G --> H["confusion matrix"] H --> I["F1 93.10%\nRecall 100%\nPrecision 87.07%"] H --> J["FP/FN image review"] The public and field data are not described as 60,198 interchangeable training images. The public set supplies breadth; the 198 field images provide a limited check against lighting, surface, camera, and domain differences.
3. Model evolution The project report records three stages.
Stage Approach Decision reason 1 DenseNet121 baseline affected by the reported 2:8 imbalance 2 DenseNet + Mask R-CNN combination compatibility and expected-benefit gap 3 ResNet + DeiT ensemble, augmentation, threshold tuning final selected direction The case does not claim that choosing a newer architecture alone produced the final quality decision. The useful work was maintaining a common evaluation frame and reviewing where normal and defect predictions overlapped.
4. Why recall was prioritized For defect probability (p) and threshold (t), lowering (t) normally increases sensitivity but can increase false alarms. The quality tradeoff is summarized by:
[ \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}, \qquad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN} ]
[ \text{F1} = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}} ]
The recorded Recall 100% means no defect in that evaluation set was missed at the selected threshold. Precision 87.07% means some predicted defects were normal. The operating decision was therefore: protect against missed defects first, then route suspected false positives to reinspection.
5. Validation result and limits Metric Recorded result Proper interpretation Public images ~60,000 broad learning source Field images 198 limited field-condition check Recall 100% no missed defect in this evaluation set Precision 87.07% remaining false-positive cost F1 93.10% balance at the selected threshold The public material does not fully disclose product/Lot split, class counts for every defect subtype, repeated-run variance, camera-cycle time, or long-term drift. The metrics therefore support a bounded PoC, not an unconditional production KPI.
6. Production-readiness requirements Split training and validation by product/Lot to reduce leakage. Publish class-level confusion matrices and confidence intervals. Standardize camera position, exposure, focus, and illumination. Measure inference latency and missed-frame behavior at line speed. Store model version, threshold, image, Lot, equipment condition, and operator reinspection. Monitor domain drift and route disagreement cases to an active-learning queue. Require model/threshold change approval and rollback records. 7. Role relevance Manufacturing AI & data: domain-aware data separation, model comparison, threshold control, and deployment gates. Data analysis: metric definition, class imbalance, confusion-matrix interpretation, and scope-limited conclusions. Manufacturing engineering: welding-process context, reinspection workflow, MES/PLC traceability, and quality-risk ownership. The most important result is not the F1 number in isolation. It is the ability to translate a manufacturing defect risk into data boundaries, comparable metrics, a decision threshold, and an honest deployment limit.

Project at a glance This education team project connected a three-Indy7 miniature automotive assembly flow with QR product identity, YOLOv11 inspection, PLC/SCADA, MySQL/MES, a digital-twin view, and Raspberry Pi 5/Hailo-10H edge inference.
The team PDF lists ten members and the process demonstration but does not include member-level R&R. Separate portfolio material records my scope as Robot/Digital Twin. Team results are therefore not presented as individual-only achievements.
Architecture flowchart LR A["QR product ID"] --> B["MySQL / MES history"] B --> C["PLC process sequence"] C --> D["Three Indy7 cobots"] D --> E["Camera"] E --> F["Pi5 + YOLOv11"] F --> G["Hailo-10H acceleration"] G --> C C --> H["SCADA / digital-twin view"] G --> B The process shown in the report runs from QR serial registration through part input, body/window assembly, vision checks, and good/reject routing. The important data relationship is product ID → process step → robot/equipment → inspection result → event time.
Evidence-backed results Condition Team report value Interpretation 3-class r/g/b check F1 1.00 result for the presentation evaluation set 6-class normal/crack check F1 0.877 normal/crack result by color class Raspberry Pi 5 5 FPS comparison before Hailo acceleration Raspberry Pi 5 + Hailo-10H 18 FPS edge-acceleration comparison in the deck Dataset size, split, repeated-run variance, and long-duration thermal behavior are not fully disclosed. These numbers do not prove universal production accuracy or sustained line-speed performance.
Technical decisions Keep AI decisions behind PLC checks The vision result should include request ID, completion state, prediction, confidence, model version, and error state. A PLC confirms that the result belongs to the current product and remains within timeout before transitioning the physical sequence.
Treat edge FPS as one validation dimension The 5→18 FPS comparison shows acceleration potential. Production readiness also requires conversion-fidelity checks, camera latency, preprocessing/postprocessing time, temperature, restart recovery, and missed-frame handling.
Keep the digital twin observational A synchronized 3D view can help explain robot and process state, but it does not replace safety circuits, coordinate calibration, or physical validation. Control authority remains in the PLC, robot controller, and safety system.
What is and is not claimed Public evidence supports the team process flow, QR/MySQL relationship, vision Ladder and communications Ladder, MES direction, two F1 values, and one edge-FPS comparison. It does not support:
continuous production deployment or OEE improvement; separate model-performance values not reproduced in the team report’s direct comparison table; a separate speed claim that conflicts with the team report’s comparison table; a completed Omniverse production deployment; individual-only ownership of every team result. Career relevance and next steps Robot teaching/overhaul experience informs coordinate and physical-state validation. Battery-line FAT/SAT informs staged checks before automatic operation. MES setup experience informs the product/equipment/model/event data contract.
Next steps are product/Lot-based dataset splits, class confusion matrices, long-duration Hailo benchmarking, PLC/Vision handshake regression tests, correlation IDs across robot/PLC/Vision/MES, and a replayable hardware-free test environment.
This case is valuable because it connects traceability, robot sequence, model evaluation, edge inference, and MES evidence in one manufacturing flow while keeping team roles and evidence limits visible.

Portfolio summary: Problem–Role–Action–Result–Evidence Item Verified scope Problem Process sequences and parameter assumptions could only be checked late with physical equipment, while PLC, SCADA, and virtual-model data integrity was hard to review in advance. Role In a ten-person team, I worked in the Digital Twin group on AI-model selection/training, communications setup, and technical research. Ladder and SCADA implementation belonged to other team members and is not presented as my individual work. Action I mapped the Factory I/O–PLC–SCADA–OPC UA data path, reviewed the DQN control candidate, and defined the boundary between control, monitoring, and AI-assisted optimization. Result The team integrated process flow, Ladder/Factory I/O, SCADA, web, and AI-extension concepts into one demonstration and report. The cited 50–75% setup reduction and 50% expansion-labor reduction are expected benefits/targets, not measured factory outcomes. Evidence The team report’s R&R table, architecture, result, and expected-benefit slides; no dedicated public source repository. Resume bullets Owned AI-model selection/training and OPC UA communications scope in a ten-person manufacturing-DX project that connected Factory I/O, PLC, SCADA, and a virtual commissioning scenario. Converted battery-line FAT/SAT experience into failure-oriented checks covering missing sensors, communication delay, restart conditions, and safe PLC authority. Kept the report’s 50–75% setup and 50% expansion-effort figures as pre-production targets rather than presenting them as measured plant savings. Interview STAR Situation: High-capital equipment creates late discovery risk because control logic and data integrity are difficult to test before physical trial. Task: My scope was to define where AI and communications fit so that control and monitoring layers used consistent data without giving AI unrestricted equipment authority. Action: I organized the OPC UA data flow, reviewed DQN as an optimization candidate, and kept deterministic control and safety checks inside the PLC boundary. Result: The team produced an integrated simulation and report. Quantified values remained expected benefits until controlled before/after measurement is available. 1. What the project is The project models a Giga Press factory context through four responsibilities:
edge acquisition and signal normalization; PLC sequence, interlock, and safe-state control; SCADA state, alarm, and history visibility; Factory I/O virtual commissioning and fault-scenario checks. It is a team PoC and design scenario. It does not claim that a production Giga Press, its safety PLC, hydraulics, or complete physical dynamics were commissioned.
2. Architecture and design boundary flowchart LR A["Sensors / switches / actuators"] --> B["Arduino / Raspberry Pi\nacquisition · filtering · normalization"] B --> C["PLC\nsequence · interlock · safe state"] C --> D["SCADA\nstate · alarm · history"] C <--> E["Factory I/O\nvirtual commissioning"] C --> F["OPC UA data path"] F --> G["Web / MES / AI candidates"] The control boundary matters. Edge devices may collect and normalize data, and AI may recommend parameters, but emergency stop, door interlock, sequence permission, and communication-timeout behavior remain deterministic PLC/safety responsibilities.
3. Data contract Exposing physical PLC addresses directly to every consumer would make a small I/O change ripple through SCADA and reporting. The scenario therefore uses a logical tag model.
Field Purpose equipment_id Stable equipment identity signal_name Human-readable process signal value Boolean, numeric, or state value quality Good, delayed, disconnected, or invalid timestamp Event ordering and freshness mode Auto, manual, or maintenance state OPC UA is useful when meaning, quality, and hierarchy must be shared upstream. Modbus/TCP remains a simpler candidate for constrained register exchange. The article treats them as interface choices subject to device and system requirements rather than claiming every protocol was production-deployed.
4. Implementation sequence Define normal process steps together with stop, timeout, and restart conditions. Build an I/O list and a logical tag dictionary. Separate reusable command/status/alarm/interlock blocks from equipment-specific exceptions. Treat communication loss as a quality state and require PLC re-authorization after recovery. Run Factory I/O scenarios for normal cycles, missing completion, duplicate sensors, and delayed actuators. Present process state, alarm cause, and communication freshness together in SCADA. Place AI at the optimization/recommendation boundary, not as an unrestricted safety controller. 5. Validation and result interpretation Scenario What to inspect Example pass condition Normal automatic cycle state transition and completion no undefined transition Sensor chatter duplicate commands one validated event Communication loss quality and safe transition timeout alarm; no automatic restart Actuator incomplete blocked next step cause is visible Manual/auto switch mode conflict transition requires a valid state Module addition change impact shared interface limits edits The public report proposes 50–75% shorter setup and 50% lower expansion effort as expected benefits of virtual commissioning and Ladder modularization. It does not provide controlled plant before/after measurements, so those values are not listed as achieved results.
6. Why this case matters for manufacturing roles Manufacturing engineering: process sequence, FAT/SAT thinking, interlocks, and change-impact checks. Manufacturing AI & data: signal quality, OPC UA, AI-placement boundary, and traceable virtual validation. Data analysis: tag definitions, timestamp/quality interpretation, and test-result separation from forecasts. 7. Limitations and next steps Add hardware-in-the-loop tests using actual I/O and safety requirements. Version the tag specification and formalize the OPC UA information model. Automate regression scenarios and issue a machine-readable test report. Add MES work-order, lot, and quality traceability. Validate network segmentation, access control, and audit logs. Measure any setup or engineering-effort improvement with a controlled baseline before using it as an achieved KPI. The technical value of this case is not a large target number. It is the discipline of separating physical control, data acquisition, monitoring, virtual verification, and AI so that each layer can be tested and its evidence stated honestly.

Portfolio summary: Problem–Role–Action–Result–Evidence Item Verified scope Problem Industrial Markdown and ad-hoc frontmatter accumulated duplicate keys, unresolved relationships, weak provenance, and non-portable paths that reduced retrieval trust. Role As the designer and implementer of this public project, I created the v9 data contract, deterministic migration/validation CLI, JSON-LD/OWL/SHACL release, Neo4j hybrid retrieval, and evidence-citation boundary. Action I defined YAML 1.2-compatible authoring and JSON Schema validation, bound normalized body SHA-256 and provenance, then separated heading-aware chunks, vector/full-text search, RRF, graph expansion, reranking, and grounded generation. Result The public v9 release validates 4,602 nodes, 1,904 provenanced assertions, and 4,448 internal relations. Its report records ok=true, errors=0, warnings=2, while preserving 137 unresolved/external relationships and 134 local-path findings as explicit limitations. Evidence Public source, README, schemas, release manifest, migration/validation reports, tests, and deployment documentation. Resume bullets Migrated 4,602 Korean-English industrial knowledge documents into a strict YAML v9 contract with JSON Schema, normalized body hashes, provenance, and relationship validation. Generated JSON-LD/OWL/SHACL release artifacts containing 1,904 provenanced assertions and 4,448 internal relationships while preserving 137 unresolved relationships as warnings instead of guessing links. Implemented a Neo4j hybrid retrieval design combining vector and full-text search, reciprocal-rank fusion, graph expansion, reranking, and source-heading citations. Reached a public release validation result of errors=0 and warnings=2, with non-portable local paths redacted during GraphRAG ingestion. Interview STAR Situation: A growing knowledge vault contained duplicate identity patterns, broken references, untraceable claims, and an invalid hand-maintained graph map. Task: Keep Markdown human-editable while creating one machine-verifiable semantic contract for release and retrieval. Action: Separate YAML authoring, JSON Schema validation, JSON-LD exchange, OWL/SHACL semantics, deterministic migration, release manifests, and hybrid Neo4j retrieval. Result: Produced a public v9 release for 4,602 nodes and 1,904 assertions. The report exposes unresolved relationships and path warnings rather than hiding data-quality debt. 1. The data problem Industrial knowledge is not trustworthy merely because it is stored in Markdown. Retrieval quality degrades when:
one concept has several unstable identifiers; parsers interpret duplicate YAML keys differently; relationships point to missing or ambiguous targets; claims have no source, locator, or integrity binding; local absolute paths or secrets enter an index; vector similarity is used for every exact term and relationship question. HeungTology addresses the complete path from document → data contract → semantic release → retrieval → cited answer.
2. Architecture flowchart LR A["Markdown + YAML v9"] --> B["JSON Schema + body hash"] B --> C["JSON-LD 1.1 release"] C --> D["OWL 2 RL + SHACL"] B --> E["Heading-aware chunks"] E --> F["Qwen3 Embedding\n2560D"] F --> G["Neo4j vector + full-text"] G --> H["RRF + allow-listed graph expansion"] H --> I["Qwen3 Reranker"] I --> J["Grounded answer with [S#]"] Four contracts remain separate by design:
YAML is the constrained human-authoring format. JSON Schema 2020-12 validates document and release structure. JSON-LD 1.1 is the canonical exchange representation. OWL 2 RL, SKOS, PROV-O, DCAT 3, and SHACL carry and validate semantics. 3. Canonical node contract Group Key fields Purpose Identity UUID, legacy IDs, slug, title stable entity resolution Classification node type, domain, tier, tags filtering and analysis Lifecycle status, version review and release state Provenance authors, source refs, body hash, reviewer traceability Relations broader, related, instance-of graph paths Assertions subject, predicate, object, evidence claim-level support Retrieval aliases, expected queries, trust, embedding profile search behavior Validation schema version, status machine gate Duplicate YAML keys, anchors, aliases, merge keys, custom tags, non-string keys, and non-JSON values are rejected. The normalized UTF-8 body is hashed and compared with provenance metadata.
4. Migration and validation The v9 migration is deterministic: parse the legacy source, generate stable identity, normalize classification, resolve references where a unique target exists, calculate body hashes, validate every transformed node, and only then allow --write. It produces an ID map and machine-readable migration report.
The public report records:
Metric Result Scanned / migrated nodes 4,602 / 4,602 Parse errors 0 Duplicate IDs 0 Provenanced assertions 1,904 Internal relations 4,448 External/unresolved relations 137 Validation errors 0 Validation warnings 2 The two warnings are operational boundaries: unresolved external relationships remain explicit instead of being attached to a guessed internal node, and 134 local body paths are redacted during GraphRAG ingestion.
5. Hybrid retrieval design Vector search helps with semantic similarity; full-text search helps with equipment codes, standards, and exact industrial terms; graph expansion supports relationship questions. Their incompatible raw scores are not directly added.
Retrieve vector top-k candidates. Retrieve title, alias, heading, and body full-text candidates. Fuse ranks with reciprocal-rank fusion. Expand allow-listed one-hop graph relationships. Rerank the candidate context. Pass source paths and headings to generation. Require [S#] citations and state when evidence is insufficient. 6. Data-analysis value This case demonstrates analytical work before visualization:
define stable units, dimensions, and lifecycle states; distinguish “a document exists” from “a supported assertion exists”; quantify unresolved and ambiguous relationships; separate blocking validation errors from improvement warnings; compare vector, lexical, and graph retrieval roles; preserve uncertainty and provenance in downstream answers. 7. Manufacturing relevance Battery and automation work repeatedly links process conditions, equipment signals, quality documents, defects, causes, and actions. The graph model transfers that field reasoning into a data contract. QCP/P-FMEA/MSA experience informs claim/validation separation; MES field design informs canonical identity and provenance; FAT/SAT experience informs deterministic release gates.
8. Limitations and next steps Not all 4,602 nodes have the same depth of human review. Claims outside the 1,904 structured assertions are not automatically evidence-complete. Unresolved and ambiguous legacy references remain a quality backlog. A target DGX Spark runtime is not the same as proven continuous production operation. Retrieval quality still needs a fixed benchmark and relevance judgments. Neo4j sync and LLM answers remain read/search functions, separate from physical control authority. The central skill shown here is not simply using Neo4j. It is turning human-authored industrial knowledge into a versioned, validated, evidence-aware release while keeping unresolved quality issues visible.

Use one IndyDCP socket owner This prevents concurrent-command races and centralizes physical-control accountability.

Related tasks and work record Repository-backed work and future Omniverse/hardware validation are intentionally separate.
PDD-01 Complete Define compatibility and control-authority requirements Specified JSON invariants, socket owner, event contract, and read-only twin boundary.
Deliverable JSON, communications, and deployment design TSK-01 Complete Implement JSON round-trip layer Preserved Waypoint, program-tree, move references, and unknown fields across reload.

Portfolio summary: Problem–Role–Action–Result–Evidence Item Verified scope Problem Partial edits to Conty JSON could break Waypoint/program/move references, while multiple HMI, DB, and twin clients connecting directly to the robot would scatter command ownership and state timing. Role Designed and implemented the public Busan_Robot repository’s JSON compatibility layer, PC-HMI boundary, backend services, and operating documentation. Action Built round-trip preservation, single IndyDCP socket ownership, separate MQTT command/state topics, a MySQL worker, PLC bridge, WebSocket read-only twin, and Offline/Direct/Gateway execution modes. Result Published a frontend/backend monorepo with Docker Compose, deployment and communications documents, and a staged validation path. No unsupported latency, uptime, or collision-reduction metric is claimed. Evidence Public source and README, JSON design, PLC/MES integration, communications, setup, and deployment documents; related team PDF. Resume bullets Designed a load–edit–save–reload validation flow that preserves Conty/APK JSON Waypoint, program-tree, and move references. Centralized IndyDCP physical sockets in one Robot Controller and separated MQTT command, result, realtime, connection, and error topics. Split a CustomTkinter HMI, MySQL DB worker, PLC bridge, and WebSocket digital twin into independent service boundaries with Docker Compose documentation. Added Offline UI, Direct, and MQTT Gateway modes so JSON and UI behavior can be checked before physical robot connection. Interview STAR Situation: Reference damage in a robot program file and concurrent socket access can compromise both compatibility and physical-control accountability. Task: Preserve the teach-pendant format while allowing PC editing and let HMI, DB, and twin consumers share one trustworthy robot state. Action: Define JSON round-trip invariants, make Robot Controller the single IndyDCP owner, and route other components through explicit MQTT events. Result: Published a reproducible HMI/backend structure and operator documents. Omniverse remains a future read-only adapter rather than an unverified production claim. 1. What the system does The system reads Neuromeka Indy7 Conty/APK JSON, displays and edits its hierarchy, supports a virtual play path, writes compatible JSON, and separates physical robot commands from data consumers.
Four design decisions define the project:
preserve the original tree and reference graph during round-trip conversion; allow only Robot Controller to own IndyDCP sockets in gateway mode; separate one-shot commands from repeated state streams; let HMI, DB, and a read-only twin consume the same published state. 2. Architecture flowchart LR UI["Python / CustomTkinter HMI\nJSON edit · virtual play · command request"] -->|"robot/command"| MQ["Mosquitto MQTT"] MQ --> RC["Robot Controller\nsingle IndyDCP owner"] RC --> RA["Indy7 A"] RC --> RB["Indy7 B"] RC --> RC3["Indy7 C"] RC -->|"result · realtime · error"| MQ MQ --> UI MQ --> DBW["DB Worker"] --> DB[("MySQL")] MQ --> DT["Digital Twin service"] --> WEB["Read-only WebSocket viewer"] PLC["PLC master"] --> PB["PLC Bridge\nmonitor / event"] --> MQ MQ -.-> OV["Future read-only Omniverse adapter"] The UI handles operator interaction. Robot polling, database writes, PLC monitoring, and WebSocket delivery are long-running operations and therefore stay outside the GUI event loop.
3. Conty JSON compatibility The public compatibility model centers on four blocks:
info: tool, TCP, coordinate, and base settings; wpList: taught Waypoints with stable IDs; program: a parent/child execution tree; moveList: speed, acceleration, blending, and Waypoint references. Valid JSON syntax is not enough. The loader and serializer must preserve these invariants:
every referenced Waypoint exists; program id/pId hierarchy is not broken or cyclic; unknown extension fields are retained; meter/mm conversions occur at one boundary; the saved file reloads into the same operation order; an applied TCP can be read back before motion continues. Unknown nodes are preserved but not executed blindly. Compatibility and execution authority are separate decisions.
4. Single socket ownership If the UI, DB, and twin each poll the robot, they can observe different moments or compete for a connection. Gateway mode gives Robot Controller one physical socket per robot. It publishes state once and lets consumers subscribe.
Flow Topic Responsibility HMI → controller robot/command one-shot operator request controller → HMI robot/result command outcome controller → consumers robot/realtime repeated state stream controller → consumers robot/connection connection state controller → consumers robot/error control/communication fault PLC Bridge → consumers plc/event family monitored PLC events The WebSocket twin reads state and does not publish Home, Zero, or Stop commands. A future Omniverse adapter should follow the same read-only boundary until separately validated.
5. Execution modes Mode Use Connection behavior Offline UI JSON and interface checks without equipment no automatic connection Direct lab test without Docker HMI uses a direct adapter MQTT Gateway recommended integrated structure Robot Controller executes requests Auto convenience fallback selects gateway/direct by environment Starting the program is intentionally different from connecting to a physical robot. The operator initiates the connection explicitly.
6. Validation boundary Check Expected evidence Load existing JSON tree, Waypoints, and settings display Save and reload references and operation order remain Unknown node original data remains; execution is blocked or confirmed Offline mode UI and editing run without devices Gateway mode controller owns commands; state is published once DB failure core robot/UI path remains isolated; local evidence is retained Web viewer realtime state updates without write authority The public repository supports these architectural claims through code and operating documents. It does not provide a basis for invented packet-loss, long-duration availability, or collision-reduction percentages.
7. Manufacturing relevance and next steps Robot overhaul and teaching experience informed the caution around TCP, coordinate units, and read-back. Battery pilot-line FAT/SAT informed staged execution from offline and virtual checks to a single low-speed command. MES and PLC experience informed the separation of command, state, process event, and history.
Next steps include a JSON Schema plus reference validator, command IDs and idempotency, MQTT authentication/TLS/ACL, replayable robot-state integration tests, and a formally calibrated read-only Omniverse mapping.
The core skill is not JSON parsing by itself. It is preserving legacy equipment compatibility while giving physical control, event transport, history, and visualization explicit and testable ownership.

Public PDD · Prototype Backlog
Project definition and execution plan The PoC prioritizes fact traceability, personal-data minimization, and structured validation before polished LLM wording.
PoC design public · dedicated source not public Project type Personal LLM application PoC My scope React, Flask, LLM boundaries and validation design Primary audience Job seekers and career-document authors Evidence level Design-led · no dedicated repository registered Problem If polished LLM wording changes dates, roles, or metrics, or sends unnecessary personal data to an external API, the resume becomes less trustworthy.
Goal Separate verified facts, private fields, target role, generated draft, and user approval while tracing every sentence back to source evidence.
Success Structured output passes schema, claim, date, and number checks; personal data is minimized; and no draft becomes final without user approval.
Scope and boundaries In scope React input/review UI and Flask validation/orchestrationStructured career facts, evidence IDs, and target-role selectionOpenAI API prompt contract, JSON schema, and claim validation Out of scope or unverified Predicting hiring success or making hiring decisionsInventing missing experience, metrics, or credentialsClaiming verified fine-tuning or performance gains Requirements Functional FR-01Every generated statement references a source experience or evidence ID. FR-02Validate model output against JSON schema, dates, numbers, and blocked claims. FR-03Only user-accepted or edited items enter the final document. Quality and operations QR-01Remove or pseudonymize contact, address, and sensitive company data before transmission. QR-02Record model, prompt, schema version, and validation result. QR-03API or format failure cannot destroy source career data. Key design decisions Prioritize structure and evaluation before fine-tuning Without a fact model and evaluation set, fine-tuning may only make errors more consistent.
Separate React, Flask, and LLM adapter UI state, privacy/business rules, and model dependency need independent replacement and testing.
Keep final human approval Career context and public wording cannot be decided completely by automated rules.
Related tasks and work record With no dedicated public repository, design-complete and implementation-verification states remain distinct.
PDD-01 Design complete Define fact, privacy, and approval boundaries Separated source fact, private field, generated draft, and final approval states.
Deliverable Public PDD and privacy boundary TSK-01 Design complete Design career-fact schema Structured experience ID, period, role, claim, evidence, and publication status.
Deliverable JSON data contract TSK-02 Needs public verification Implement React review and Flask API Input, role selection, draft comparison, approval, and API validation need dedicated public source.
Deliverable PoC application source VAL-01 Planned Test claims, dates, numbers, and privacy Automate fixtures for schema errors, invented metrics, date conflicts, and personal-data leakage.
Deliverable Evaluation set and test report NXT-01 Next Complete security and operations review Authentication, encrypted storage, deletion/retention, audit logs, and prompt-injection defenses remain.
Deliverable Security review and runbook Acceptance criteria ✓ Fact, private field, generated draft, and user approval are separated.
Met ✓ No unsupported facts or fine-tuning performance are claimed.
Met → Dedicated public source reproduces schema and claim-validation tests.
Unverified → Security, deletion, and audit controls pass an operations review.
Unverified Evidence: Only the portfolio design and GitHub project index are public today; implementation remains unclaimed until a dedicated source is registered.
Project at a glance resumOpenAI explores a narrower problem than “ask an LLM to write a resume.” It separates verified career facts, private fields, target-role selection, draft generation, and output validation so that polished wording cannot silently alter dates, employers, roles, or measured outcomes.
Area Design Frontend React form and draft review API Flask request validation and generation orchestration Data structured career facts with evidence/status fields LLM controlled prompt and optional adaptation path Safety personal-data minimization and public/private separation QA claim/date/number checks before export Why structure comes before fine-tuning Fine-tuning can make style more consistent, but it cannot repair missing or contradictory facts. The first quality gate is a structured source model.
{ "experience_id": "exp-example", "employer": "verified employer", "period": {"start": "YYYY-MM", "end": "YYYY-MM"}, "role": "verified role", "claims": [ { "statement": "bounded achievement", "evidence": "source reference", "status": "verified", "public": true } ] } Sensitive fields such as address, date of birth, phone number, credentials, or raw company documents should not be sent merely because they exist in a resume file. The public rendering model contains only approved technical facts.
Architecture flowchart LR A["Private source documents"] --> B["Local extraction / normalization"] B --> C["Verified career-fact store"] C --> D["Public-field filter"] D --> E["Target-role evidence selection"] E --> F["Flask generation request"] F --> G["LLM draft"] G --> H["Claim/date/number validation"] H --> I["Human review"] I --> J["Exported draft"] The React layer captures job target and review choices. Flask owns schema validation, field filtering, prompt assembly, and result checks. The LLM receives only the minimum evidence required for the chosen output.
Validation design The PoC treats generation as a draft process with deterministic gates.
Every employer, period, role, and number must exist in the source fact store. A claim marked unverified cannot be promoted as achieved. Conflicting date ranges produce a review item instead of an automatic choice. Private fields are removed before the external-model boundary. Unsupported superlatives and invented tools are flagged. Korean and English outputs must point to the same fact IDs. Role-specific selection One fact store can support several views without rewriting history.
Manufacturing engineering: line setup, FAT/SAT, process conditions, yield, quality systems. Manufacturing AI & data: Vision AI, PLC/SCADA/MES, digital twin, data contract, deployment boundary. Data analysis: dataset definition, metric choice, validation, data quality, provenance, decision impact. The application changes ordering and explanation, not the underlying facts.
Current limits The current portfolio does not provide a public repository or evaluation dataset for this PoC. A generated resume still requires human review. Style consistency is not evidence accuracy. Fine-tuning must not include unredacted personal or confidential documents. Quality needs a fixed evaluation set containing contradictions, missing evidence, and sensitive fields. Next steps Publish a sanitized schema and sample dataset. Add claim-level provenance and output-to-source links. Build deterministic tests for dates, numbers, language parity, and privacy filtering. Compare prompt-only, retrieval-assisted, and fine-tuned variants on the same evaluation set. Record user acceptance/edit distance rather than relying only on LLM-style metrics. This case demonstrates an important AI application principle: structured facts, privacy boundaries, and deterministic validation come before fluent generation.
